assignments.brief_reason: Explicitly says hate/bad-language removal happened but the original-vs-mirror pairing was not influential.
States criteria were respect/fact-based rather than side, and pairing helped judge similarly across political versions.
Profanity/curses are treated as unnecessary and thereby increase removal.
Allows content when it is opinion without expletives, implying curse words are a removal trigger.
Influence comes from constructive debate value, not primarily from threats/toxicity thresholds or pair-consistency fairness.
Removal is triggered by disrespect/personal attacks/bullying, consistent with removing toxic harassment.
Decision cue is whether language is argumentative vs truthful, not clearly mapped to the threat/toxicity removal themes.
Removes for vulgar/toxic content and Nazi analogies while allowing general debate/criticism.
Focus is on discussion/engagement vs insulting, without clear explicit reliance on threats/violence exceptions or pair fairness.
Removal likelihood increases with hostility, blatant insults, and cursing (toxic/inflammatory tone).
Mentions using the pairing for political-context interpretation; not explicitly about consistent application across sides or about threat/toxicity exceptions.
General reasonableness threshold for keeping both versions, without clear tie to the codebook moderation-standard or toxicity/threat exceptions.
Directly compares egregiousness across the pair; this is not the theme of applying identical standards regardless of viewpoint.
Removes hostile/insulting comments to preserve dialogue safety (especially for minors), aligning with removing toxicity/hostility.
Inaccuracy is used as a cue, but this is not one of the threat/toxicity or pair-standard themes in the codebook.
Invokes an overarching free-speech principle despite disagreement; no explicit threats/violence exception stated.
Multiple criteria (mutual respect/intent/thought-provoking) but not clearly about hate/bad language thresholds or pair-consistency across viewpoints.
Explicitly targets shutting down offensive/permanent hateful speech to enable more positive communication.
Says they focused on policy violations rather than political side, consistent with applying the same standard across both versions.
Rejects both for aggressive genuinely upsetting language; treats some cursing as ignorable—tone/language severity drives removal.
